subject: bill-to-law
title: From Idea to Law
summary: How an idea turns into a real U.S. law, and what happens when the president says no.

keys.answer: A plan for a new law, or a change to a law we already have.

options.text: A plan for a new law or a change to a law
A law that is already done
A vote by the Supreme Court

keys.prompt: Who has to vote yes on a bill before it goes to the president?
keys.answer: Both the House and the Senate, on the same version of the bill.

options.text: Both the House and the Senate
Only the Senate
Only the House

keys.prompt: The president vetoes a bill. How can it still become a law?
keys.answer: Congress votes again. If two out of three members in both the House and the Senate say yes, it becomes a law.

options.text: Two out of three in both the House and Senate vote yes
More than half of the House votes yes
The Supreme Court says yes

cards.title: Your big idea
cards.text: Say you think every school in the country should have a longer recess. Wishing won't make it a rule. Telling your teacher won't either. So how does an idea become a real law?

cards.question: The president says no to a bill. That is called a veto. What happens next?

options.text: The bill is gone forever
Congress can vote again and still make it a law
The Supreme Court votes on it

cards.reveal: Congress can vote again. If two out of every three members in both the House and the Senate say yes, it becomes a law anyway.

cards.title: A bill is an idea on paper
cards.text: A bill is a plan for a new law, or a change to an old one. The idea can come from a member of Congress. It can also come from regular people who ask their member to help. Then a member puts the bill forward.
cards.example: In this example, a class writes to their member of Congress about recess. If the member likes the idea, they can turn it into a bill.

cards.title: A small group checks it first
cards.text: Next, the bill goes to a committee. That is a small group of members. They study the bill, talk about it, and can change it. If they don't send it on, the bill stops there.

why.q: Why send a bill to a small group first?
why.a: A small group can study the bill closely and fix it before everyone votes on it.

cards.title: Two votes, one bill
cards.text: Congress has two parts, the House and the Senate. Both must vote yes. In the House, a win is 218 out of 435 votes. In the Senate, it is 51 out of 100.
cards.example: Sometimes the House and the Senate pass different versions. Then they work out the differences. Both vote again on the same bill.

cards.title: The president decides
cards.text: Last, the bill goes to the president. If the president signs it, it is a law. If the president says no, that is a veto. Then Congress can vote again. If two out of three in both the House and the Senate say yes, it is a law anyway.

why.q: Why let Congress beat a veto?
why.a: So one person can't stop a law that most of Congress strongly wants. Each part can push back on the other.

cards.prompt: In "Three Branches, One Team" you learned that the veto is a check. Who checks the president's veto?
cards.model: Congress does. If two out of three members in both the House and the Senate vote yes, the bill becomes a law anyway.

cards.question: Making a law takes many steps and lots of yes votes. Is that good or bad? Think of one reason for each side.
nudges: What if a bad idea could become a law fast?
What if a good idea took years?

questions.q: Where does a bill go first, before the whole House or Senate votes?

options.text: To a committee, a small group that studies it
options.why: Yes! The committee studies it and can change it.

options.text: Straight to the president
options.why: Not yet. The president only gets it after both parts of Congress say yes.

options.text: To a judge
options.why: No. Judges aren't part of making a bill.

questions.q: A bill passes the House. What has to happen next?

options.text: The Senate has to pass it too
options.why: Right. Both the House and the Senate must say yes.

options.text: It is a law right away
options.why: Not yet. The Senate and the president still get a turn.

options.text: The House votes on it again
options.why: No. Next it goes to the other part of Congress, the Senate.

questions.q: The president vetoes a bill. Congress votes again, and two out of three in both the House and the Senate say yes. What happens?

options.text: It becomes a law
options.why: Yes! That is called beating, or overriding, the veto.

options.text: It is gone forever
options.why: No. Enough yes votes let Congress beat a veto.

options.text: The president gets to vote again
options.why: No. Once Congress overrides the veto, the bill is a law.

cards.prompt: Explain this to someone at dinner in 3 sentences.

video.title: Facts of Congress - How a Bill Becomes Law
video.why: A one-minute cartoon that follows a bill from an idea, to a committee, to both parts of Congress, to the president.

sources.title: How laws are made
sources.supports: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law; ideas can come from members of Congress or from people who petition their member; committees research, discuss and change bills; both chambers must pass the same version; the president can sign or veto; Congress can usually override a veto.

sources.title: The Legislative Process
sources.supports: A representative sponsors a bill; it goes to a committee and moves on only if released; a simple majority passes it, 218 of 435 in the House and 51 of 100 in the Senate.

sources.title: Article I (Section 7: the Presentment Clause)
sources.supports: Article I, Section 7: a vetoed bill becomes law if two thirds of each House vote to pass it again.
